body: INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J.- This common judgment shall decide the afore-titled writ petitions, as they involve similar questions of law and facts. W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, 2. In all the petitions, the petitioners seek, inter alia, a declaration that their non-promotion be set aside and that the impugned letters, whereby their supersession and deferment were communicated, be declared illegal and without lawful authority. The petitioners in Writ Petitions No. 4563, 1221, and 1286 of 2025 have, in addition, sought a declaration that the proceedings of the Central Selection Board (“CSB”) meeting held on 11 th th March, 2025 be declared coram non judice and, thus, of no legal effect.

The facts of writ petition No. 2409/2025 are that the petitioner, Dr. Mutahir Shah, was inducted into the Health Department, Government of Balochistan, through the Public Service Commission and appointed as Medical Officer (BS-17) on 31.05.2001, where after he joined PIMS in 2003 and, with the approval of the competent authority, stood finally absorbed on 01.09.2005. He was subsequently promoted to BS-18 on 20.03.2014 and to BS-19 on 08.09.2021, after serving on various significant positions. Dr. Mutahir Shah’s case was due for consideration for promotion to BS-20 as Joint Executive W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, Director, PIMS against the 80% promotion quota in the CSB meeting scheduled in August 2023, the post being vacant and the petitioner being the senior-most eligible officer, however, he was not included in the roster, where after the Executive Director, PIMS, forwarded a requisition to Respondent No. 3/Federal Public Service Commission for direct recruitment to the said post. Being aggrieved, the petitioner assailed the same through a departmental representation, which was allowed vide order dated 17.05.2024. Notwithstanding the subsistence of the said order, a fresh vacancy roster was prepared by the incumbent Executive Director, compelling the petitioner to approach the Federal Service Tribunal, which, vide judgment dated 13.11.2024, allowed the appeal, holding that the alteration in the vacancy roster was without lawful authority and a direction was made to the respondents to consider the petitioner for promotion in the ensuing CSB. Thereafter, the Executive Director, in his personal capacity, preferred an appeal before the Honorable Supreme Court although Respondent No. 2/Ministry of National Health Services did not to challenge the said judgment, which was dismissed. During this period the respondents held the CSB in March of 2025, wherein the petitioner’s case was considered for promotion however he was deferred for the reasons reproduced below:- “The Departmental Representative apprised the Board that the officer is being considered for the first time. He informed that the service record of the officer is complete in terms of PERs and declaration of assets. He shared that the officer is exempted from mandatory trainings being an officer of specialist cadre. The DR also apprised the Board about general reputation of the officer visa-vis his integrity, professional competence and promotion potential to higher position. The Board deliberated upon the service profile, PERs, general reputation and the additional information of the officer, inter alia, with reference to assessment of his professional conduct, integrity and other attributes mentioned in the Objective Assessment Form. A consensus emerged that the officer has mixed reputation vis-à-vis his professional competence and integrity: thus, there is a need to further watch the performance of the officer. The Board. therefore, decided to recommend the officer for deferment on performance watch till the next CSB in line with Rule 7(d) of the Civil Servants Promotion (BS- 18 10 BS-21) Rules, 2019.”

W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, B. ARGUMENTS OF THE PARTIES 7. The learned counsels for the petitioners contended that the entire evaluation process stands vitiated by a manifest disregard of the prescribed statutory framework governing promotions. They argued that the CSB superseded the petitioners without affording them an opportunity of hearing or confronting them with any adverse material, in utter disregard of Rule 23 of the Civil Servants Promotion (BS-18 to BS-21) Rules, 2019 (“Promotion Rules, 2019”), which mandates disclosure of reasons for supersession, and this nondisclosure strikes at the heart of the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness, as the petitioners have been deprived of complete knowledge of the grounds of their supersession and, consequently, of any meaningful opportunity to question or challenge the assessment. Thus, the opacity surrounding the award of marks renders the decision arbitrary and undermines the transparency mandated by the Promotion Rules 2019 and settled judicial precedents. They submitted that this action exhibits a capricious and unfettered exercise of discretion, in violation of section 24A of the General Clauses Act, 1897 (“GCA, 1897”) and is contrary to Articles 4 and 10-A of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (“Constitution”), which guarantee fairness, reasonableness and due process. Learned counsels argued that the quantification mechanism, designed to ensure objectivity and structured discretion, has been abandoned in favor of unbridled and unguided subjective assessment which is contrary to the ten parameters enumerated in Schedule-IV of the Promotion Rules 2019. In particular, undue and overriding emphasis has been placed on alleged notions of “integrity” and “average competence”, without reference to any tangible material or the overall service record. 15. I have given anxious consideration to the arguments of the learned counsel for the parties and perused the record with their able assistance. C. OBJECTIONS I. MAINTAINABILITY 16. It is necessary to first address the objection of maintainability raised by the learned Additional Attorney General who contended that this Court’s jurisdiction was ousted by Article 212 of the Constitution in matters relating to the terms and conditions of service of the civil servants and that these matters fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the FST which is competent to decide the matter. However, the same is devoid of merit. It is settled law that assessment of fitness and suitability are excluded from the jurisdiction of the FST under section W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, 4 of the Federal Service Tribunals Act, 1973 and the jurisdiction of High Court is not barred, where the issue pertains to fitness for promotion. As a consequence, the bar contained under Article 212 is not attracted to the present cases and the same has been categorically held by the superior courts in numerous cases.

Moreover, it is reiterated that while a party may raise objections to maintainability, such objections must accord with settled law, including binding judicial interpretation. In the absence of any change in the statutory framework, the repetition of such objections, contrary to consistent precedent, is unwarranted and wastes judicial time. It is well settled that denial of fair consideration for promotion is amenable to judicial review, and that the right to be fairly considered is distinct from the right to promotion itself, as recognized by the Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Tariq Aziz-ud-Din. II. PREMATURE CAUSE OF ACTION 17. The second objection raised, rests upon the contention that a writ petition directed against an administrative decision is premature where the formal reasons underpinning that decision have not yet been communicated to the aggrieved party. The submission, reduced to its essence, is that until reasons are furnished, no complete cause of action exists, and that the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court cannot be invoked in the absence of a discernible, communicated order. It was further urged that the subsequent communication of reasons has cured the alleged statutory violation of communication, and that the petitioners ought to have awaited that communication before approaching this Court. The objection is not devoid of initial merit, however, upon closer examination rests upon a premise that is not merely legally untenable but one that, if accepted, would visit consequences upon the civil servant that no system committed to the rule of law could sanction.

18. Before proceeding to determine the objection, it is necessary to frame it within its proper factual and legal context since an objection of this nature cannot Secretary Establishment Division vs. Aftab Ahmed Maneka, (2015 SCMR 1006). Orya Maqbool Jan vs. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary and others, (2014 SCMR 817), I.A. Sherwani and others vs. Government of Pakistan through Secretary Finance Division, Islamabad and others, (1991 SCMR 1041), Mian Abdul Malik vs. Dr. Sabir Zameer Siddiqui and 4 others, (1991 SCMR 1129).

Tariq Aziz-ud-Din vs. Federation of Pakistan, (2010 SCMR 1301) W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, be assessed in abstract and must be looked at holistically including the specific conduct of the party that raises it. The question is not simply whether, a writ petition may be filed in the absence of communicated reasons or formal decision. The question is whether, in the particular factual matrix of the present cases, where the statutory obligation to provide reasons immediately was deliberately and persistently disregarded for months, the Federation may be permitted to rely upon the very deficiency they created as a ground for non-suiting the petitioners. The question, when posed in these terms, carries within it the seeds of its own answer since, to accept the respondents’ contention would lead to an anomalous situation whereby the Federation could insulate its decisions from judicial review by simply withholding the reasons and formal decision at the initial stage, thereby stalling the accrual of cause of action. Administrative fairness demands that where a civil servant is superseded or deferred, particularly in a competitive promotional exercise, the formal decision and reasons forming the basis of such supersession or deferment be conveyed immediately. In the present matters, although the CSB concluded its deliberations in March, 2025, the reasons were communicated to certain petitioners only in September, 2025 and to others as late as December, 2025. A prolonged silence without any justification lends credence to the petitioners’ apprehension that the process lacked transparency. Thus, the delayed disclosure cannot defeat the maintainability of the petitions.

19. Even otherwise, the understanding of the Federation of the cause of action or grievance of the petitioners is misconceived. The meeting of the Board was held on 11 th –14 th March 2025, and shortly thereafter, the recommendations of the CSB were approved by the competent authority, and the petitioners were aware that they had not been promoted. The adverse outcome had thus attained finality in substance, even if the supporting reasons were not yet disclosed or the decision not communicated. The cause of action, therefore, did not rest upon the knowledge of specific grounds recorded by the CSB but upon the grievance suffered through unlawful supersession/deferment. In service jurisprudence, supersession or deferment is not a neutral event and it carries immediate consequences affecting status, seniority, and future prospects. Once that consequence materialized, the petitioners became entitled to seek judicial review on the ground that the decision-making process lacked transparency, fairness, or W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, adherence to rules. The subsequent communication of reasons in September and December 2025 i.e. months after the meeting does not retrospectively render the earlier challenge premature rather it supplements the record for purposes of adjudication.

20. Even if this Court were inclined to accept this narrow procedural objection, the delayed communication of reasons remain actionable in its own right as a breach of the administrative duty of timely and meaningful disclosure. An administrative decision that carries profound professional consequences for the affected officer and cannot be treated as incomplete and irregular merely because the reasons are supplied eventually. Procedural regularity, is not satisfied by eventual compliance but compliance within a timeframe that preserves the utility of the right being exercised. This principle finds direct expression in the maxim nullus commodum capere potest de injuria sua propria i.e. no man can take advantage of his own wrong, and is squarely applicable here since the Federation seek to benefit from the very delay they caused by contending that the absence of communicated reasons rendered the petitions premature, while simultaneously relying on the eventual communication of those reasons to suggest that the grievance has since been addressed. In such like cases, a party cannot approbate and reprobate in the same breath.

III. CONSTITUTION OF LARGER BENCH 21. The crux of the objection raised by the learned counsel for FBR Ms. Zainab Janjua is that the adjudication of instant petitions by this Court ought to be in light of the binding precedent of the Honorable Division Bench of this Court in Sikandar Hayat Maken vs. Federation of Pakistan, (2021 PLC C.S. 1450) since Maken specifically addresses all the grievances/grounds raised by the petitioners in the context of promotion to selection posts, the Promotion Rules 2019 and the law laid down by the Honorable Supreme Court in Dr. Muhammad Arif (Supra) judgment, hence, Maken is the applicable law.

22. Firstly, this Court agrees with the law set out in the Maken judgment that the Court ought not undertake strict scrutiny of the merits of the decision rendered by the CSB or second guess the opinion formed by CSB regarding the fitness of the civil servant for promotion. However, the grounds raised in therein W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, while correct are not the sole grounds for judicial review and while arbitrariness, mala fide and abuse of discretion and unfairness as set out in Maken are binding on this Court, this Court’s power of judicial review is not limited to those grounds. If this is to be the prevailing point of view, anytime a challenge is brought to an administrative action it would lead to a wholly inequitable situation whereby the courts power to grant a relief on valid and recognized ground would be curtailed since. Even otherwise, the respondent’s reliance on Maken is misconceived since these grounds are the sub grounds/sub-categories of the three major grounds for judicial review on which administrative actions can be reviewed. The nomenclature of grounds were defined by Lord Diplock in the case of Civil Service Union as “illegality” “irrationality” and “procedural impropriety” in the following manner:- “By ‘illegality’ as a ground for judicial review I mean that the decision-maker must understand correctly the law that regulates his decision-making power and must give effect to it. Whether he has or not is par excellence a justiciable question to be decided, in the event of dispute, by those persons, the judges, by whom the judicial power of the state is exercisable.

By ‘irrationality’ I mean what can by now be succinctly referred to as ‘Wednesbury unreasonableness’. It applies to a decision which is so outrageous in its defiance of logic or of accepted moral standards that no sensible person who had applied his mind to the question to be decided could have arrived at it. Whether a decision falls within this category is a question that judges by their training and experience should be well equipped to answer, or else there would be something badly wrong with our judicial system. To justify the court's exercise of this role, resort I think is today no longer needed to Viscount Radcliffe’s ingenious explanation in Edwards (Inspector of Taxes) v. Bairstow of irrationality as a ground for a court's reversal of a decision by ascribing it to an inferred though unidentifiable mistake of law by the decision-maker.

‘Irrationality’ by now can stand on its own feet as an accepted ground on which a decision may be attacked by judicial review. I have described the third head as ‘procedural impropriety’ rather than failure to observe basic rules of natural justice or failure to act with procedural fairness towards the person who will be affected by the decision. This is because susceptibility to judicial review under this head covers also failure by an administrative tribunal to observe procedural rules that are expressly laid down in the legislative instrument by which its jurisdiction is conferred, Council of Civil Service Union vs. Minister (1984) 3 All ER 935, 950-952 W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, even where such failure does not involve any denial of natural justice.”

23. These grounds provide a coherent framework and have been affirmed by the Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Asaf Fassihuddin Khan Vardag vs. Government of Pakistan, (2014 SCMR 676). Moreover, judicial review cannot be limited to certain grounds since the rights of the parties may be affected and the same has been held in the case of Dr. Akhtar Hassan Khan vs. Federation of Pakistan, (2012 SCMR 455) by the Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan in which the Court explicitly stated that, “The above are only the broad grounds but it does not rule out addition of further grounds in course of time.” Thus, in each case this Court is duty bound to measure what has been done, or not done, against the relevant statutory provisions. As such this Court is constantly involved, in an often refined exercise of interpretation of legislative provisions and the assessments of the administrative body bound to adhere to them. This is the inherent power of the court to review the legality of the action.

24. Moreover, Maken is distinguishable since these grounds of judicial review were not the subject matter before the Court. Therefore, the contention is without merit and the Impugned supersessions and deferments can be tested against the above grounds. This Court in writ petition No. 421/2022 titled Yousif Hyder Shaikh vs. Establishment Division through its Secretary, Government of Pakistan and 2 others has also observed, “In view of the above, the reading of the Federal Government of the law enumerated in Sikandar Hayat Maken is misconceived as the Court was seized of question of legality of the Promotion Rules. While upholding the vires of the Rules it was not seeking to move back the hand of the clock by holding that the CSB was empowered to undertake subjective assessment based on personal information and opinion of members comprising the CSB and such assessment would have the backing of law. The Promotion Rules were not enacted in the derogation of the law laid down in Federation Pakistan Vs. Dr. Muhammad Arif, but in its compliance. And the Promotion Rules are therefore to be given effect in consonance with the law laid down and principles highlighted in Dr. Muhammad Arif.” Moreover, the learned Divisional Bench of this Court in I.C.A No. 877 of 2024 titled Federation of Pakistan through its Secretary Establishment Division, Islamabad vs. Arbab W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, Qaiser Hamid rejected the contention that judicial interference with an order of supersession amounts to impermissible second guessing or runs afoul of the principle laid down in Sikandar Hayat Maken judgment. The Court, upon examining the record, noted that although the officer’s TERs and PERs were satisfactory and not below the prescribed threshold, the Central Selection Board had nonetheless declared him to be of “average competence” and of “questionable integrity” without any supporting material. It was further observed that no reasons were recorded as to how such adverse conclusions were reached, particularly when they did not flow from the service record and no additional material was shown to have been considered. The Divisional Bench also took exception to the procedural irregularity whereby the Board filled a single collective proforma, reiterating its earlier view that it is inconceivable for multiple members of a collegial body to arrive at identical assessments without independent application of mind. In these circumstances, the Court held that the absence of reasons and lack of demonstrable material reflected non-application of mind, thereby justifying judicial interference, and consequently dismissed the appeal in limine.

25. There is yet another aspect to the matter i.e. if the matter were to be referred to or heard by a larger Bench at this stage, either party would be effectively deprived of their valuable right to assail the judgment through an intra-court appeal. The right of appeal is not a mere procedural formality but a substantive and statutory right conferred under Section 3 of the Law Reforms Ordinance 1972, which cannot be curtailed except in accordance with law. The adjudication of these petitions by this Court in the capacity as Single Judge preserves the statutory scheme, as any aggrieved party would retain the remedy of intra-court appeal, wherein the Division Bench would naturally examine errors, if any. Conversely, the constitution of a larger Bench at the outset would foreclose such remedy altogether and this Court is disinclined to render nugatory a right expressly granted by the legislature. Moreover, the same would ensure institutional efficiency since the Single Bench undertakes detailed adjudication, thereby streamlining the scope of scrutiny at the appellate stage and conserving valuable judicial time. In these circumstances, the contention seeking constitution of a larger Bench is devoid of merit, and this Court is fortified in its W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, view that the matter be heard in the ordinary course so as to preserve statutory rights. More importantly, this Court cannot remain oblivious to the consistent disapproval expressed by the superior courts regarding the conduct of public functionaries who, instead of acting in a fair, transparent, and reasonable manner, resort to avoidable litigation at the expense of the public exchequer. In the present cases, the objections raised by the respondents, particularly on grounds of maintainability and constitution of larger Bench, appear to be nothing more than an attempt to prolong the lis and compel the petitioners to engage in needless and repetitive litigation. Civil servants, who form the backbone of the administrative machinery, operate within limited means and ought not to be driven from pillar to post for enforcement of rights already recognized by the authoritative pronouncements of the superior courts.

IV. LIMITED SCOPE OF JUDICIAL REVIEW DUE TO THE PRINCIPLE OF ADMINISTRATIVE DEFERENCE 26. The second core argument advanced by the learned counsel for FBR was that in light of the principle of administrative deference, the scope of the judicial review in matters of promotion to selection posts is inherently limited since, CSB comprises senior officers of the highest echelon of the civil service and has been specifically constituted to assess and select officers for promotion on a best of the best policy. Therefore, its determinations being based on institutional expertise are entitled to due deference for which reliance was placed on Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. [467 U.S. 837 (1984)]. This principle was enunciated by the United States Supreme Court’s in the case of Chevron Inc. (ibid) wherein the Court held that, “the power of an administrative agency to administer a congressionally created…..program necessarily requires the formulation of policy and the making of rules to fill any gap left, implicitly or explicitly, by Congress. If Congress has explicitly left a gap for the agency to fill, there is an express delegation of authority to the agency to elucidate a specific provision of the statute by regulation. Such legislative regulations are given controlling weight unless they are arbitrary, capricious, or manifestly contrary to the statute. Judges are not experts in the field, and are not part of either political branch of the Government. Courts must, in some cases, reconcile competing political interests, but not on the basis of the W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, judges’ personal policy preferences. In contrast, an agency to which Congress has delegated policy-making responsibilities may, within the limits of that delegation, properly rely upon the incumbent administration’s views of wise policy to inform its judgments. While agencies are not directly accountable to the people, the Chief Executive is, and it is entirely appropriate for this political branch of the Government to make such policy choices….”. In furtherance of this, the learned counsel contended that the principle is not just restricted to the United States, in fact the same is also recognized in Pakistan particularly in matters involving specialized expertise, complex policy decisions, or technical assessments which are referred to as polycentric issues and under this principle, the judiciary acknowledges its own institutional limitations and generally defers to the judgment of the executive and administrative bodies acting within their domain of expertise. However, this argument is devoid of merit for twofold reasons. Firstly, and quite frankly, the understanding of the principle by the respondents is misconceived. At this juncture it is apposite to delineate the contours of the doctrine commonly referred to as “Chevron deference.” This doctrine entails a two-part test in which the judges first examine the wording and the context of the statute in question to see if Congress’s intent is clear. If it is, then the matter is settled and the agency is obliged to follow the letter of the law. However, if the statutory language is ambiguous i.e. if it has two or more reasonable interpretations, the reviewing court must defer to the agency’s choice in how to carry out the law. The rationale behind such deference was that expert agencies, accountable to an elected president, are better suited than federal judges to make the policy choices that Congress left open. The first reason why the understanding of this doctrine is misconceived is because the said doctrine postulates that, in circumstances where if Congress has not directly addressed the question at the center of a dispute, a court was required to uphold the agency’s interpretation of the statute as long as it was reasonable. However, in the present matter the language of the law is unequivocal. The foremost requirement is that the case of an eligible officer must be considered strictly in accordance with the statutory rules and notified criteria and any deviation whether by applying extraneous considerations or ignoring prescribed benchmarks vitiates the process. The Board is bound not merely to “consider,” but to consider in the manner mandated by law.

Secondly, the Supreme Court of U.S.A has overruled Chevron in the case of Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 114 S.Ct. 224 (2024). After the ruling in Loper Bright Enterprise’s case, the courts are allowed to not defer to agencies and independently interpret the statue in question. Even otherwise, administrative deference cannot act as a cloak and is not a license to act arbitrarily, nor does it clothe an authority with the power to depart from the express mandates of the law under the guise of expert judgment or institutional discretion. Where a statutory framework prescribes a definite procedure, lays down specific criteria, or imposes an unambiguous obligation upon an authority, the question before the court is no longer one of policy or expertise. It becomes, purely and simply, a question of law. In such circumstances, the court is not trespassing upon the domain of the executive by holding the authority to the letter of the statute. It is performing its most fundamental constitutional function, which is to ensure that no body, howsoever senior or specialized, acts in excess of, or in derogation of, the authority conferred upon it by law. It follows, therefore, that where illegality or arbitrariness is established, deference must yield to legality. An administrative body cannot invoke its own expertise to justify a departure from statutory requirements, for expertise pertains to the substance of a decision made within the law, not to the power to act outside it. To permit otherwise would be to render the rule of law subordinate to institutional convenience, a result that no constitutional order can countenance. The deference owed to administrative bodies is thus a qualified and conditional deference, one that endures only so long as the authority acts within the bounds of its lawful mandate and in accordance with the principles of fairness and rationality that undergird all valid administrative action.

29. Moreover, the applicability of this principle by the respondents is misconceived since the principle of deference in Pakistan’s legal context has only been applicable on polycentric issues and issues which can potentially W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, impact any government endeavors to promote investment and enhance security measures.

This principle if understood correctly, states that the policy and administrative issues often referred to as polycentric issues requiring specialized expertise are left to the discretion of competent authorities who are better positioned to record opinions on such matters, and courts should exercise restraint on such matters, however, even these are subject to judicial review if any glaring illegality or violation of fundamental rights exists .

30. Another aspect to the matter is that the principle of administrative deference and the doctrine of separation of powers operate within carefully circumscribed boundaries, and their application is confined to those categories of decisions in respect of which the legislature has expressly or impliedly conferred upon an administrative or executive body a discretion rooted in technical expertise, institutional knowledge, or complex policy considerations that are inherently polycentric in nature. It is in recognition of this limitation, and not in abdication of judicial duty, that courts have historically exercised restraint in interfering with such decisions. Thus, it needs to be reiterated that this Court remains fully cognizant of the settled legal position that the ultimate determination of fitness, suitability and capacity to shoulder higher responsibilities lies within the exclusive domain of the Board, and that while exercising jurisdiction under Article 199 of the Constitution, this Court cannot reappraise merit or substitute its own opinion for that of the competent authority. Judicial interference with the decisions of selection boards is therefore permissible only in exceptional circumstances, and the threshold for such interference is accordingly high. That threshold is, however, crossed where the Board fails to give meaningful consideration to an officer’s case for promotion and further omits to record or communicate plausible reasons for his supersession/deferment. It is precisely upon this ground that the petitioners have invoked the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court, contending that they were denied the right to fair and just consideration for promotion. It is trite law that the right to be considered for promotion, fairly and justly, is a right wholly Muhammad Azam v. Province of Punjab etc., (2022 CLC 532), Muhammad Umais v. Cantonment Board Rawalpindi and others, (PLD 2022 Lahore 148) and Syed Faisal Mehboob v. Federation of Pakistan and others, (2022 CLC 1153)

Ibid W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, distinct from the right to promotion itself. The former is an enforceable entitlement whereas the latter remains, at all times, subject to the discretion of the competent authority. This distinction has been unequivocally affirmed by the Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Tariq Aziz-ud-Din (Supra) and applies with full force to the facts of the present case. It is therefore paramount to clearly delineate the scope and nature of the review being undertaken by this Court. This Court is not engaged in an exercise of reappraising the comparative merit of the petitioners, nor is it arrogating to itself the function of the Board by promoting any officer or directing his promotion. The judicial review is confined, strictly and wholly, to an examination of the legality, rationality and procedural propriety of the Impugned Decision. Where a decision of a statutory body is shown to be the product of non-application of mind, is unsupported by plausible reasoning, or has been reached in derogation of the procedural safeguards prescribed by law, it falls within the recognized jurisdiction of this Court to intervene. Such intervention does not encroach upon the institutional domain of the Board rather it reaffirms the foundational principle that all public functionaries must act fairly, reasonably and justly and that power and discretion must be exercised in accordance with law.

34. It is a settled principle of law that where a statute has entrusted a function to a specific body, that function must be exercised by that body and by no other. De Smith, in Judicial Review of Administrative Action, (7th edn., 2013), states the principle with characteristic precision, “A discretionary power must, in general, be exercised only by the public authority to which it has been committed. It is a well-known principle of law that when a power has been conferred to a person in circumstances indicating that trust is being placed in his individual judgment and discretion, he must exercise that power personally unless he has been expressly empowered to delegate it to another.” Similarly, in the case of ARY Communications Limited through duly Authorized Officer vs. Council of Complaints, Islamabad through Secretary and 2 others, (PLD 2022 Sindh 552) the Court held:- “The rule of reasonableness is so embedded in the jurisprudence that even where statute confers arbitrary powers on any authority, it is to be read in such statute that the authority while exercising its discretion shall act reasonably. The reasonableness of any action by an authority is eroded where it acts with improper motive, on irrelevant considerations, or without regard to relevant considerations, allowing the dictates of others instead of applying its own independent and judicious mind or delegates unless provided by law or surrenders its power to any other authority whether it is superior, equal or inferior to him.”

W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, Related to the rule against acting under dictation is that against unsanctioned delegation, derived from the maxim delegatus non potest delegare, which lays down that a delegate cannot further delegate the power to someone else. This is to ensure that when a specific person or body is given a statutory discretion, the discretion is exercised by that very person or body and not by someone else. In Muhammad Yusuf Ali Shah v. Federal Land Commission, Government of Pakistan, Rawalpindi and 2 others 1995 CLC 369 a learned Division Bench of the Lahore High Court articulated the principle as follows:

"Before we proceed to deal with the contentions of the parties in regard to this point, we feel it necessary to state that it is a settled proposition of law that when a power is conferred on a particular person then that person can neither transfer its exercise to another person nor can exercise it without application of his mind to the facts and circumstances of that case. What is required, is that he has to exercise that power with application of his independent mind to the facts and circumstances of that case regardless any extraneous/dictative influence."

16. Ergo, even in matters where the opinion of a recommendatory body is envisaged, the exercise of the statutory power ultimately remains that of the designated authority, and its decision is to necessarily be made for advancing the purposes of the statute, supported by valid reasons. In other words, if a statute expressly confers a statutory power on a particular body or authority or imposes a statutory duty on the same, then such power must be exercised or duty performed, as the case may be, by that very body or authority itself and none other. However, if the body or authority exercises the statutory power or performs the statutory duty acting at the behest, or on the dictate, of any other body or person, that would constitute an abdication of the statutory mandate and any decision taken on such basis would be contrary to law and liable to be quashed.”

This must be viewed with the fact that such input was thereafter acted upon by the Board in arriving at its conclusions of “average competence” and “questionable integrity” which renders the import of unlawful input in the entire decision-making process that the Promotion Rules 2019 neither contemplate nor permit. The illegality, in short, is manifest in majority of the petitions in both categories without exception, and this Court is unable to countenance the results so produced. The structural and fundamental illegality in the Departmental Representative’s conduct in all the cases is that Schedule-VI requires all material to be submitted in prescribed and authenticated forms prior to the meeting, constituting the evidentiary record before the Board and oral inputs tendered at the meeting that traverse the boundaries of those forms are inherently unverifiable, carry no documentary authentication, and afford the affected officer no opportunity whatsoever to know the case against him or to offer any rebuttal, which is a direct violation of audi alteram partem. Moreover, the same is in direct violation of the decision making since the Departmental Representative is not merely a functionary, rather he is an institutional voice capable of being influenced by departmental relationships and hierarchical loyalties. The Board, as a statutory body, exists precisely to transcend such influences and to bring independent collective judgment to bear upon the civil servants promotions.

The CSB is a creature of statute and of rules framed thereunder, and its authority to assess and determine the fitness of an officer for promotion exists only within the framework those Muhammad Asad Islam Madni vs. Federation of Pakistan, W.P.
