F. ABUSE OF DISCRETION 37. The second glaring illegality is the abuse of discretion which naturally correlates to irrationality , since when an administrative decision is bereft of any cogent, tangible, or record-based foundation, the same constitutes an abuse of discretion and is arbitrary if unsupported by reason. The jurisprudence governing administrative discretion makes it clear that a discretionary decision must rest upon rational reasons supported by evidence and directed to the statutory purpose; actions that fail to meet this threshold are regarded as arbitrary. In the case of Montgomery Flour and General Mills Ltd., Montgomery vs. The Director, Food Purchases, West Pakistani (PLD 1957 Lah, 914) the following was observed:- “It should be remembered that no discretion vested in an executive officer is an absolute and arbitrary discretion. The discretion is vested in him for a public purpose and must be exercised for the attainment of that purpose. Even though there be no express words in the relevant legal provision to that effect, the discretion is always circumscribed by the scope and the object of the law that creates it and has at the same time to be exercised justly, fairly and reasonably.”

Similarly in Abid Hasan vs. PIAC, (2005 SCMR 25) the Court observed:- “If the judicial administrative organs of the State while applying the law were to discriminate between man and man and exercise what may be characterized as arbitrary authority in singling out some persons for discriminatory treatment they would be acting counter to the ideal of equality before law which has been proclaimed by the framers of the Constitution in the first part of the clause of Article 5 an Article which declares that all citizens are equal before law. It would thus be noticed that notion of human equality had emerged as a reaction to abhorring artificial 'distinctions between man and man or between one class of men and another class based on consideration, inter alia, of personal likes and. dislikes -under the garb of discretion.

The ground of irrationality, as classically expounded by Lord Diplock in Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374, denotes a decision which is so outrageous in its defiance of logic or of accepted moral standards that no sensible person who had applied his mind to the question to be decided could have arrived at it. This formulation is commonly denominated as Wednesbury unreasonableness, which originated from the celebrated English authority in Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation [(1947) 2 All ER 680], also cited as [1948] 1 KB 223.

W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, 14. In his Treatise 'Discretionary Powers' which is Legal Study of Official Discretion D.J. Galligan has acknowledged that "the general principles that discretionary decisions should be made according to rational reasons means, (a) that there be findings of primary facts based on god evidence and (b) that decisions about the facts be made for reasons which serve the purposes of the statute in an intelligible and reasonable manner" According to the celebrated author, the actions which do not meet these threshold requirements are arbitrary, and may bee considered a misuse of powers. (Emphasis provided).”

38. Where adverse assessments are recorded without reference to primary facts, and where acknowledged satisfactory service records are discarded without any articulated reason, the exercise of discretion crosses from lawful selectivity into the realm of arbitrariness. The respondents have not put forth any substantial ground or material/record that would show that such allegations are supported by any tangible material. It was laid down in the case of Dr. Muhammad Arif and Muhammad Zafeer Abbasi that the consideration of an officer for promotion is to be based not only on the relevant law and rules but also on some tangible material, which could be lawfully taken into consideration. Schedule IV limits the sources of objective assessment to the dossier, PERs, TERs, and documentary evidence. Allegations regarding integrity must therefore be supported by tangible material forming part of the service record. Where a member of the Board disagrees with the recorded ACRs of an officer, reasons supported by cogent material must be expressly recorded. A decision of a statutory Board must bear a rational nexus between the material available on record and the conclusion drawn therefrom. Rationality in administrative law is not satisfied by the mere existence of an opinion or perception, rather it requires that the opinion/perception be demonstrably founded upon relevant considerations and supported by discernible evidence. Allegations regarding integrity must therefore be supported by tangible material forming part of the service record. The use of the word ‘repute’ is itself signals that the finding rests on impression and hearsay rather than on any verifiable entry in the service record. Such a conclusion would amount to substituting evidence for speculation and objective evaluation for subjective suspicion. Similar view has been adopted Secretary Establishment Division vs. Dr. Muhammad Arif, (PLC (CS) Note 66) Muhammad Zafeer Abbasi vs. Government of Pakistan, (2003 PLC (C.S.) 503) W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, by the courts in numerous cases, in which the civil servants were considered for promotions. Moreover, it would offend the well-established maxim nemo fit repente turpissimus i.e. no one becomes dishonest all of a sudden. This maxim signifies that integrity, whether sound or tainted, reveals itself over time through a consistent course of conduct. An officer’s dossier reflects a cumulative record of years of service, performance, and conduct. Such a comprehensive career profile cannot lawfully be nullified by a cryptic observation or personal impression since this would amount to arbitrariness. Even otherwise, if the integrity of an officer is genuinely in question, the natural and logical course available to the competent authority is to initiate disciplinary proceedings so that the matter may be adjudicated in accordance with the law. To use the same for not recommending the officer to the next grade while allowing him to continue in same reflects an exercise in which discretion is weaponized to momentarily portray a civil servant as an officer of doubtful integrity for the limited purpose of denying him his due progression in service, only for that supposed blemish to vanish thereafter without any formal inquiry or punishment. The absence of any such proceedings, despite a finding adverse enough to deny promotion, renders the action suspicious. The only reasonable inference that can be drawn is that such adverse remarks or assessments are nothing more than a colorable exercise of discretion.

39. It should be remembered that no discretion vested in an executive office is absolute and it is vested for a public purpose and must be exercised for the attainment of that purpose. Discretion in essence is the power given to a person with authority to choose two or more alternative, when each of the alternatives is lawful. However, when one of the alternatives is not lawful, there is no discretion to choose it even though, it may be chosen in practice. It essentially translates that discretion is limited to what is authorized, legal and within the effective limits of the officer’s powers. As such, in the instant matter, it was discretion to be exercised within the prescribed formulaic assessment of Objective Assessment Form. The very nomenclature of “Objective Assessment” is indicative of a process that is material-based, record-oriented, and insulated from personal preferences. The Rules consciously bifurcate the evaluative process into two distinct stages i.e. a subjective assessment at the level of the W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, Reporting Officer, who, by virtue of direct supervision, is best positioned to form qualitative judgments reflected in the PERs and an objective, quantitative assessment at the stage of promotion, to be undertaken by the Board on the basis of the recorded material. This legislative design is both rational and purposive, ensuring that personal impressions are confined to those best placed to form them, while the DSB operates within a structured and verifiable framework.

40. It is also manifest from the record that the CSB in multiple cases simultaneously recorded that the petitioners possessed acceptable Performance Evaluation Reports and Training Evaluation Reports, yet proceeded to record adverse observations on Integrity. These two propositions cannot coexist on any rational basis. A service record acknowledged to be acceptable cannot, without more, sustain a finding of the most adverse integrity categorization available under the framework. The Board offered no explanation for this incongruence and identified no departmental inquiry, no adverse entry in the Performance Evaluation Reports or Annual Confidential Reports, and no other verifiable material upon which the integrity finding could rest. The contradiction was recorded without acknowledgment and the conclusion was reached without justification. This is precisely the scenario condemned by the Court in the cases of Tariq Aziz ud Din (Supra) and in the reported judgment of this Court in W.P. No. 989 of 2025 titled “Muhammad Asad Islam Madni vs. Federation of Pakistan, through Secretary Establishment Division and others” where it was held that consideration of an officer for promotion must be based not only on the relevant law and rules but on some tangible material relating to merit and eligibility which can be lawfully taken note of. The right to consideration, the Court declared, is neither illusory nor a perfunctory ritual. That declaration carries particular weight in the present context. Where an adverse finding on integrity is recorded in the complete absence of any substantiating material from the service dossier, the right to consideration has been reduced to precisely the kind of empty formality that the Supreme Court condemned. This falls squarely within the Wednesbury formulation of irrationality, being a conclusion so divorced from the material before the Board that no authority directing itself properly to the relevant considerations could have arrived at it. The simultaneous acceptance of two irreconcilable propositions, without any attempt to explain or W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, resolve the contradiction between them, is the antithesis of rational decision making and abuse of discretion. The acknowledged satisfactory performance was simply set aside, without explanation and without reason. The only explanation that was afforded was “average competence”.

41. With regards to competence, the same also appears to be based on unlawful and irrelevant consideration. Such an observation finds no reference to to the record and support from the record. The only inference that can be drawn is that the same is premised on upon hearsay, gossip, rumour, or the personal knowledge or impressions of Board members. The personal knowledge of an officer’s competence is confined to the Reporting Officer, who records the PER. Members of the Promotion Board do not possess such personal knowledge. Consequently, the Rules restrict the Board to objective evaluation based solely upon PERs, TERs, and the dossier, while subjective assessment remains the exclusive domain of the Reporting Officer. Furthermore, the overriding effect accorded to alleged “impeccable/questionable integrity” and the reliance upon a solitary “Competence” grade mirrors the very mischief condemned in the Dr. Arif case. An officer’s dossier reflects a cumulative record of years of service, performance, and conduct. Such a comprehensive career profile cannot lawfully be nullified by a cryptic observation or personal impression recorded without reference to material. Any such action amounts to arbitrariness and cannot be sustained. An administrative determination that is unsupported by material, unexplained in its divergence from the official record, and untraceable to any lawful source of information, is irrational because it lacks a logical foundation, fails the test of reasonableness, and renders the decision-making process arbitrary in substance as well as in form.

42. Furthermore, the grading of “Good” in PERs or TERs, by its very nature and design, is neither adverse nor disqualifying. A positive weightage is assigned to a “Good” grading, which acknowledges it as a satisfactory and creditable standard of performance. To convert a “Good” grading into a ground of supersession is to introduce, by implication, a disqualification which the rulemaking authority has consciously refrained from prescribing. What is expressly recognized as meritorious cannot be treated by administrative fiat as a blemish since the express inclusion of “Good” within the graded framework necessarily W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, excludes its treatment as an adverse factor. The maxim omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta presumes official acts to have been done rightly and where a reporting officer has consciously recorded “Good,” the CSB cannot, without cogent basis, treat it as an implicit deficiency. The comparison of a “Good” grading against a “Very Good” or “Outstanding” standard, when undertaken in isolation and without comparative analysis among candidates, is irrational. It is one thing for the Board, after undertaking a comprehensive and comparative assessment of all eligible officers standing at par, to prefer those with superior aggregate merit. It is quite another to treat “Good” as inherently deficient simply because a higher grade exists in the grading spectrum. If “Good” is measured not against the merit of competing candidates but against an idealized and self-referential benchmark of “Very Good,” the very purpose of graded evaluation is rendered illusory. Such reasoning would reduce the graded scale to a single operative benchmark, thereby nullifying the allocation of marks to intermediate grades and creating an inequitable standard where only the highest category becomes meaningful. Such an approach is arbitrary in substance, discriminatory in effect, and incompatible with the principles of structured and rational decision-making that govern promotion in public service. In these circumstances, the consideration by the CSB cannot, by any stretch of reasoning, be characterized as fair, lawful, or amounting to “meaningful consideration.” Rather, it represents a mechanical and arbitrary exercise of power, devoid of transparency, objectivity, and adherence to statutory safeguards. Such a process, being fundamentally flawed, stands vitiated in law and is liable to be set aside.

G. PROCEDURAL IMPROPRIETY 43. Another aspect of meaningful consideration is whether the consideration is free from procedural impropriety which operates through two distinct but overlapping mechanisms. First is the failure to observe statutory procedural requirements such as communication of reasons and the same vitiates the Impugned Decisions since it is manifest from the record that there exists complete failure to communicate reasons to the superseded officers in the manner and to the extent prescribed by the statutory framework governing the promotion process. Schedule IV of the Promotion Rules 2019 prescribes a structured quantified framework comprising ten distinct attributes, each carrying W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, a maximum of three marks and aggregating to a total of thirty marks, the evident legislative purpose of which is to structure and discipline the discretion reposed in the Selection Board, to ensure that the evaluation of each officer proceeds upon identifiable and objectively assessable criteria, and to guarantee that the process retains a character of fairness, transparency, and accountability that arbitrary or impressionistic assessments cannot provide. The following are the ten parameters given in Schedule-IV of the Promotion Rules 2019: “i. Output and quality of work ii. Variety and relevance of experience iii. Professional expertise iv. Personality Profile v. Conduct, Discipline and Behavior vi. Leadership vii. Estimated Potential for Middle/Higher Management viii. Integrity / General reputation / Perception ix. Commitment to Public Service x. Teamwork”

44. This structured framework is not ornamental but facilitates improvement for the civil servant. It is established beyond controversy that in all the cases before this Court, the petitioners were informed of an adverse assessment solely with reference to the attribute of integrity and general reputation, which carries a maximum of three marks out of the total of thirty prescribed by Schedule IV, while no reasons whatsoever were communicated to any of the petitioners concerning the remaining nine attributes aggregating to twenty-seven marks. This selective and fragmentary disclosure is not a technical deficiency susceptible of being overlooked or cured rather it is a substantive violation that strikes at the root of the statutory scheme and renders the entire process opaque, arbitrary, and legally unsustainable. The purpose of a quantified multi-attribute framework is precisely to prevent the reduction of a complex, career-long evaluation to a single conclusory label, and by confining their communication to a finding on integrity/reputation alone while maintaining silence on the remaining nine criteria. In essence the CSB reduced the statutory framework of thirty marks across ten attributes to a single adverse characterization, thereby defeating the very object for which the legislature constructed and prescribed that framework. It must be observed that where rules require an authority to assess and record performance against specified parameters, the obligation to W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, communicate the outcome of that assessment to the person affected is not a matter of administrative grace or discretion but flows as a necessary legal consequence from the nature of the framework itself. A statutory scheme that requires graded assessment against defined criteria necessarily and axiomatically implies that the person subjected to that assessment must be informed of the findings made against each criterion, for without such communication the statutory framework becomes an instrument of concealment rather than a guarantee of fairness.

45. Moreover, the consequences of this failure extends beyond the immediate decisions under challenge and touch upon rights of a continuing and fundamental character. The purpose of communicating reasons against each of the prescribed attributes is that it serves the vital function of enabling a civil servant to know wherein he has been found wanting, to address those deficiencies in the conduct of his duties, and to improve his performance and standing with a view to his future promotional prospects. A civil servant who is informed only that he has been adversely assessed on integrity, while being kept entirely in the dark as to his assessed standing on output and quality of work, variety and relevance of experience, professional expertise, personality profile, conduct discipline and behavior, leadership, estimated potential for higher management, commitment to public service, and teamwork, is deprived not merely of the ability to challenge the decision that has been made against him but of the ability to transform or improve his professional conduct and development in a manner informed by the findings of the competent authority. This deprivation is particularly grave because the attributes prescribed by Schedule IV are not peripheral or ornamental to a civil servant’s career rather they define the very dimensions along which professional growth is measured and along which the case for promotion is ultimately assessed. To withhold findings on these dimensions is to leave the civil servant in a condition of enforced ignorance with respect to his own standing in the service, unable to make good any deficiency of which he has not been informed, and thereby to render the statutory framework of structured grading to an opaque screen behind which adverse assessments may be made and withheld without consequence. Such an outcome is irreconcilable with the rule of law, with the fundamental right to a fair W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, consideration, and with the specific mandate of the Promotion Rules 2019, and this Court is therefore bound to hold that the Impugned Decisions, being founded upon an assessment process from which statutory transparency was systematically withheld, cannot be sustained in law.

46. Furthermore, Section 24A of the GCA, 1897 stipulates that statutory power must be exercised reasonably, fairly, justly, and for advancement of the purpose of the enactment. The Superior Courts have dilated upon section 24 of GCA, 1897 and enunciated the principle that the executive authorities while exercising discretion must give reasons for its decision through a speaking order. The requirement to articulate reasons is neither a mere procedural formality nor an empty ritual; rather, it is a substantive safeguard designed to demonstrate that discretion has been exercised judiciously, objectively, and with due application of mind. Reasoned decision-making ensures that affected persons are apprised of the basis of the action taken, facilitates meaningful judicial review, and acts as a restraint against arbitrariness or caprice. Applying the facts of the instant matter to the test laid down by the Superior Courts essentially amounts to a blatant disregard of section 24 of the GCA, 1897. Hence, this Court is disinclined to treat any consideration as “meaningful” due to the failure to effectively record reasons which as stated above is meant to ensure fairness and transparency. H. ENFORCED IGNORANCE 47. This Court turns next to another dimension of the matters that has received insufficient attention during submissions i.e. the right to timely reasons. The respondents appear to proceed upon the assumption that the communication of reasons is a bureaucratic step to be completed at some point, with its precise timing being of no particular legal consequence, however, that assumption is fundamentally erroneous. The delay in communicating reasons is not a matter of mere procedural formality rather a statutory requirement. Rule 23 of the Promotion Rules 2019 mandates:- “23. Communication of reasons of deferment and supersession.— The civil servants deferred or superseded shall, immediately after the recommendations of the CSB, DSB and DPC have been approved by the respective appointing authority, invariably be informed about the reasons of their deferments and supersessions.”

W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, 48. A bare perusal of rule 23 reflects that the said provision is mandatory in nature and the reasons have to be immediately provided after the same have been approved by the appointing authority. However, the time frame in which the reasons have been communicated to the petitioners can in no way be termed as immediate or reasonable. This must be viewed in conjunction with the fact that the purpose of communicating reasons for supersession/deferment is not only to ensure compliance with administrative fairness but rather it equally serves a substantive function, namely to enable the officer to understand wherein his performance, conduct, or record was found wanting, so that he may address those deficiencies in the period before the next promotional exercise. This remedial dimension of the right to reasons is not a procedural luxury and is integral to the officer’s right to fair consideration in future promotional exercises and a delayed communication of reasons while it may satisfy the letter of this principle but defeats its spirit entirely.

49. In the present cases, the Board concluded its deliberations in March 2025 and the next sitting of the Board is expected approximately one year thereafter, the window available to an officer to identify and address shortcomings is, at its most generous, twelve months. When reasons are withheld for months of that window, communicated only in September or December 2025, the officer is deprived of half or more of the only remedial period available to him before he faces the same evaluative process once again. He does not know whether the criticism pertains to his annual performance reports, his general reputation within the service, some specific adverse entry, a disciplinary proceeding, or some other criterion applied by the Board. He is left in a state of enforced ignorance and speculation since he cannot purposefully orient his conduct, cannot address adverse material on his record, cannot demonstrate improvement in the areas the Board found deficient, and cannot request correction of any factual error that may have influenced the decision. The damage, by the time reasons are communicated, is therefore not merely past. It is ongoing and accumulating with each passing month of silence.

50. The consequences of this enforced ignorance compound further when the Board reconvenes. An officer who has spent six of his twelve remedial months unaware of the basis for his supersession arrives at the next promotional exercise W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, having had, in practical terms, only half the opportunity to demonstrate improvement that the process presupposes. This is not a technical or abstract prejudice. The Board’s own framework contemplates that officers are assessed across a defined period and that improvement is both possible and practical. To withhold reasons for half of that period is, in effect, to deny the officer the practical ability to participate meaningfully in his own professional improvement. It deprives him not only of the chance to improve his record but also of the chance to serve the public with the full awareness and directed purpose that knowledge of his shortcomings would have generated. An officer informed of his deficiencies in March will work differently, and the law may reasonably presume more effectively, than one left uninformed until September or December. The delay thus inflicts a dual injury, for it harms the officer’s promotional prospects while simultaneously withholding from the public the benefit of an officer operating at his informed best. Here the maxim commodum ex injuria sua nemo habere debet (no one can take advantage of their own wrong) applies with particular force. The Board cannot, at the next promotional sitting, rely upon the officer’s failure to demonstrate improvement during a period in which it was the Federation’s fault that denied him the knowledge necessary to improve. To permit it to do so would be to allow an authority to derive advantage from the very wrong it committed, a result that is as inequitable in principle as it is impermissible in law.

51. The right to reasons is not an end in itself. It is the gateway to a set of substantive rights and practical remedies that can be exercised only if reasons are furnished in time. To reduce it to a formality and to treat it as a box to be ticked whenever convenient is to misunderstand its function entirely. The function is evident from the fact that the promotional exercise is a recurring one. The CSB on average meets approximately once in a year or two. An officer who is superseded at one sitting has, in principle, the opportunity to demonstrate improvement before the next. But that opportunity is not self-executing. It requires the officer to know what the Board found wanting. He must know whether the criticism goes to his performance reports, to a specific adverse entry, to a disciplinary matter, to a general assessment of his suitability, or to some other factor that the Board considered material. Without that knowledge, his W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, effort to improve is directionless. He cannot address a deficiency he has not been told of. He cannot seek correction of an error he does not know exists. He cannot rebut an adverse finding he has not been shown. The period between successive sittings of the Board is, therefore, not merely a temporal interval, it is a remedial window, and its value is entirely dependent upon the officer knowing, at its commencement, what he is required to address. The months that passed in enforced ignorance cannot be restored. The improvement that might have been demonstrated cannot now be retrospectively attributed to a period during which the officer was kept in the dark. It is the loss of a defined, measurable, and irrecoverable period of time during which the officer, had he known the basis of his supersession, might have taken steps that would have materially altered his position at the next sitting of the Board. That loss cannot be undone by the belated supply of reasons.

52. Moreover, the consequences of this enforced ignorance do not exhaust themselves within the officer’s individual career. They extend to the public he or she serves. An officer who is aware of the specific dimensions of his professional shortcomings will, as a matter of reasonable presumption, conduct himself and discharge his functions with a deliberateness and a directed purposefulness that an officer kept in ignorance cannot replicate. Equally, the overarching principle of salus populi suprema lex (the welfare of the people shall be the supreme law) reinforces this conclusion, for the welfare of the public is not served by a system that keeps its officers uninformed of their deficiencies and then measures them against a standard of improvement they were structurally prevented from meeting. The communication of reasons is a circumstance of substantive relevance and any delay is contrary to settled principles of fairness and transparency. In this regard, this Court has no hesitation in holding that the reasons must be communicated within 15 days after the approval from the competent authority.

I. LEGALITY OF DEFERMENT 53. The case of the petitioner/Dr. Mutahir Shah (W.P. No. 2409/2025) presents perhaps the starkest illustration of denial since no reasons have been communicated to him till date and the reasons have only been communicated through comments at a belated stage. The reasons recorded by the CSB for W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, deferring the petitioner are set out in the minutes and are reproduced for ease of reference:- “The Departmental Representative apprised the Board that the officer is being considered for the first time. He informed that the service record of the officer is complete in terms of PERs and declaration of assets. He shared that the officer is exempted from mandatory trainings being an officer of specialist cadre. The DR also apprised the Board about general reputation of the officer visa-vis his integrity, professional competence and promotion potential to higher position. The Board deliberated upon the service profile, PERs, general reputation and the additional information of the officer, inter alia, with reference to assessment of his professional conduct, integrity and other attributes mentioned in the Objective Assessment Form. A consensus emerged that the officer has mixed reputation vis-à-vis his professional competence and integrity: thus, there is a need to further watch the performance of the officer. The Board. therefore, decided to recommend the officer for deferment on performance watch till the next CSB in line with Rule 7(d) of the Civil Servants Promotion (BS- 18 10 BS-21) Rules, 2019.”

54. It is manifest from the record that the departmental representative confirmed that the seniority list as available with the proposal is not sub judice and no issue related to it is pending. Moreover, the departmental representative apprised that no other issue restrains the consideration of the proposal. Thereafter, the CSB considered the case of the officer and after discussion recommended the petitioner for deferment due to a mixed reputation of his professional competence and integrity. It is also apparent from the minutes that the Departmental Representative transgressed the boundaries of Schedule-VI by apprising the Board about the “general reputation of the officer vis-à-vis his integrity, professional competence and promotion potential to higher position”, which is an evaluative function that, for the reasons elaborated in the preceding paragraphs, was not his to perform. This infirmity, standing alone, suffices to vitiate the process. However, the infirmity in this case does not end there, and the case presents two further and independent grounds on which the deferment cannot be sustained. The first concerns the legal architecture of rule 7(d) of the Promotion Rules 2019 under which the petitioner was deferred. The question that now arises is whether the petitioner’s deferment by CSB on performance watch under rule 7(d) withstands the test of rationality and procedural propriety. For ease rule 7(d) is reproduced below:- W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, “7. Conditions for deferment. — On consideration for promotion in order of seniority, a civil servant shall be recommended for deferment, if— (d) the CSB, DSB or DPC wants to further watch performance of the officer for any reason to be recorded in writing:
Provided that period of performance to be watched under this clause shall not exceed twelve months;”

55. A perusal of the rule above reflects that it bestows a broad latitude of power on the CSB to defer a civil servant if it wants to watch the performance of the civil servant. The proviso appended to the clause further circumscribes this discretion by prescribing a definitive outer limit. It stipulates that the period for which the officer’s performance may be watched shall not exceed twelve months. It is intended to be a temporary and reasoned measure, aimed at facilitating a final and fair assessment within a fixed timeframe, and not a device to indefinitely postpone or arbitrarily withhold promotion. However, the effect of the main provision is that such opinion must not remain subjective or unarticulated as the rule expressly mandates that the reasons necessitating further watch be recorded in writing, thereby ensuring transparency and enabling subsequent scrutiny. In the present case the sole substantive ground recorded by the Board is a “mixed reputation vis-à-vis his professional competence and integrity.” However, no specific deficiency in the service record is identified, no adverse entry, no disciplinary proceeding, no penalty, and no finding referable to any documentable fact is cited. The expression “mixed reputation” is, in terms, the language of general impression and hearsay and the very kind of material that a requirement of written reasons is designed to exclude from the decisionmaking process. A statutory obligation to record reasons is not discharged by recording the conclusion that reputation is mixed rather it is discharged by recording the material from which the conclusion is drawn since the former is assertion and the latter is reasoning. Rule 7(d) requires the latter, and the minutes disclose only the former.

56. Secondly, this must be viewed in conjunction with the fact that a panel of only one officer from BS-19 (i.e. the petitioner who was the senior most) was placed before the CSB for consideration to the promotion to the post of Joint Executive Director. This is not a case where the Board made a comparative selection from a field of candidates and found others more meritorious since W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, there was no field. There was one officer, one vacancy, and a direction from the Federal Service Tribunal requiring his consideration. In this context, a deferment amounts, in practical effect, to a denial of promotion that the Tribunal had directed to be given fair consideration, achieved not through any finding of ineligibility or specific disqualification, but through the invocation of a general and unsubstantiated reputational impression. The right to reasons is not an end in itself rather it is the gateway to a set of substantive rights and practical remedies that can be exercised only if reasons are furnished with specificity and in time. The consequences of this enforced ignorance do not, moreover, exhaust themselves within the officer’s individual career. They extend to the public he serves. An officer who is aware of the specific dimensions of his professional shortcomings will, as a matter of reasonable presumption, conduct himself with a directed purposefulness that an officer kept in ignorance of the Board’s concerns cannot replicate. In this regard, this Court has no hesitation in holding that where a deferment is ordered under rule 7(d), the reasons recorded in writing must be communicated to the officer within fifteen days of the approval of the competent authority and must contain reference to all ten parameters enumerated in Schedule-IV, so that the remedial window between successive sittings of the Board is not rendered illusory. In the case of Dr. Mutahir Shah, no such communication was made, no specific deficiency was identified, and the deferment rested on nothing more than a reputational impression conveyed through an unauthorized channel. The Impugned Deferment accordingly cannot be sustained and is set aside.

J. CORAM NON JUDICE 57. This Court shall now address the third question framed i.e. whether the proceedings of CSB are coram non judice. The learned counsels for the petitioners in writ petitions No. 1221, 4563, 1286 of 2025 contended that the absence of two co-opted notified members of the Board from the proceedings of the CSB renders the proceedings coram non judice. However, no meaningful assistance was rendered in this behalf and even otherwise this argument is devoid of merit. Having examined the said record with due care, this Court is satisfied that the language of the applicable rules, read in its plain and natural sense, does not postulate or require any specific quorum as a condition precedent for the W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, proceedings of the CSB. The Promotion Rules 2019 do not prescribe any minimum numerical requirement for a valid meeting and the omission of any quorum requirement in the Promotion Rules 2019 reflects a deliberate legislative choice since it ensures continuity of administrative processes and prevents disruption due to the absence of any member. Moreover, the determination of the institutional composition of consultative or advisory process is, in the first instance, a matter of administrative design falling within the policy domain of the Establishment Division with the approval of Prime Minister, so long as the exercise remains within law and is not arbitrary, or mala fide, the same is lawful. Moreover, the framework, in which the Prime Minister acts as the appointing authority and approves the composition of the Board is significant. It would be contrary to administrative reality to presume that the Prime Minister would deliberately approve the recommendations of CSB which comprised of an incomplete quorum. The Prime Minister in his capacity as appointing authority was fully aware that the said individuals were not in the meeting since these individuals belonged to Baluchistan and could not be part of the proceedings due to the incident of Jaffar Express on 11.03.2025 meaning thereby that the Prime Minister authorized the CSB to continue with the consideration. The governing principle in relation to implied authorization and approval is well-established in law i.e. the authorizing authority must be fully cognizant of and fully informed regarding the acts performed in its name and on its behalf, and the legal and practical consequences of such acts must be attributable to and borne by such authority. The challenge to the legality of quorum is therefore repelled.

58. There is a further contention advanced on behalf of the petitioners belonging to the Police Service of Pakistan that warrants separate consideration. In the specific instance of these three petitions, the civil servants are officers of the Police Service of Pakistan, and for the consideration of PSP officers, the serving Inspectors General of all provinces were specifically co-opted onto the Board. The learned counsel for the petitioners urged that the presence of the Inspector General of Balochistan was essential for a fair, informed, and meaningful evaluation of the petitioners, inasmuch as the provincial IG was directly acquainted with their service records, performance, and professional conduct; and that his absence deprived the Board of critical input, resulting in an W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, incomplete and, by implication, a prejudiced assessment of their cases. However, this contention is legally untenable.

59. The function of the Central Selection Board is an evaluative one, but it is an evaluation grounded in, and circumscribed by, the record. The Board is required to assess the officers on the basis of their dossiers, Performance Evaluation Reports, Training Evaluation Reports, quantification scores, and other documentable and formally verifiable criteria that constitute the service record. The deliberative process of the Board is, by design, an exercise of the application of structured judgment on the basis of objective material and not a forum for the receipt of personal impressions, individual knowledge, or subjective assessments derived from private acquaintance. The argument that the Board was deprived of “critical input” by the Inspector General’s absence necessarily implies that what the Inspector General would have contributed was something beyond and outside the record i.e. some personal knowledge or private assessment that the record itself does not contain. But that, paradoxically, is precisely the kind of input that the law does not permit to be acted upon and this argument cuts both ways. To allow a member of the Board to exercise discretion on the basis of personal knowledge alien to the record is to open the door to the very arbitrariness and unfettered discretion that the structured quantification framework of the Promotion Rules 2019 is designed to foreclose.

60. However, the above is not to be read as a diminution of the institutional wisdom and value that a co-opted member and in particular, the Inspector General of the relevant province brings to the deliberations of the Board. Since the co-option of the serving Inspectors General was not a formality or a ceremonial gesture rather it is a considered administrative design, reflecting the recognition that officers of a specialized service such as the Police Service of Pakistan operate within a distinct professional environment, and that those who have directly superintended their functioning in the field are better placed to contextualize their service record than those who have not. The presence of the Inspector General adds a layer of institutional knowledge to the Board’s deliberations that is, in principle, valuable and desirable. The input of his knowledge does not necessarily mean that the Board acts on it rather it is meant to supplement and highlight the record and ensure that the record reflects it. The W.P.’s No. 2409/2025, 3171/2024, 3172,3173,3260 to 3267/2025,3643,3644,4587,4999,5543,5544, distinction, however, is between the desirability of a member’s presence and the legal indispensability of it. A co-opted member whose presence enriches the quality of deliberation is not, by that reason alone, a member without whom the Board is constitutionally or legally incompetent to proceed. The Promotion Rules 2019 prescribe no quorum, and the legal threshold for valid proceedings is therefore met by the constitution and notification of the Board, not by the attendance of every member so notified. The Court’s jurisdiction in judicial review extends to what is legally mandatory and no what is desirable. The argument that if the Inspector General’s input, had it been provided on the record would have produced a different outcome in these three petitions is a matter of conjecture but what is not conjecture is that his absence, in the legal framework governing these proceedings, does not render them coram non judice. This must be viewed with the lens that his unavoidable absence was occasioned, as the record discloses, by the tragic incident of the Jaffar Express on 11.03.2025 and while the continuation of the CSB’s meeting in his absence may be perhaps unwise, but it does not cross the threshold of illegality. Thus, this argument is without merit. Even otherwise, the non-promotion of the petitioners in these three petitions is not in accordance with the law on the grounds of illegality, abuse of discretion and procedural impropriety and have been dealt above.
61. In view of the foregoing discussion, these petitions are allowed. The Impugned Decisions are set aside.
